source.title: Channel Training & Estimation for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces: Exposition of Principles, Approaches, and Open Problems

accepted.question_text: How can a reconfigurable intelligent surface element be completely deactivated so that its reflection is nulled with respect to all angles, and what physically realizable RIS design or control model would make that all-angle nulling possible for channel-training methods that rely on turning elements off?

evidence.quote: Nulling the reflection of an RIS element with respect to all angles has not been adequately addressed in the literature and remains an open issue. See Section IX for further details.

accepted.question_text: For RIS-aided sparse channel estimation in mmWave or THz settings, what pilot signals and RIS training states are optimal for sparse recovery, and what training-based capacity results follow when the channel is estimated through sparse recovery rather than standard linear estimation?

evidence.quote: A thorough characterization of optimal training with sparse recovery, and the associated training-based capacity (as in Sec. IV) is still open.

accepted.question_text: When RIS reflection coefficients are updated only infrequently and the practical implementation therefore requires coding across many coherence intervals of the slower channel, should RIS configuration and beamforming be optimized for outage capacity or throughput rather than ergodic capacity, and how should that optimization be formulated?

evidence.quote: the practical implementation of these techniques requires an outer code that goes across many coherence intervals of the slower channel. In many such cases, outage capacity or throughput may be a more suitable metric for optimization, and there is room for future work in this area.

accepted.question_text: For RIS-aided systems that use statistical channel state information and optimize long-term performance under infrequent RIS updates, what achievable-rate inner bounds can be derived for the ergodic-rate optimization problem, instead of relying only on outer bounds?

evidence.quote: In this area, there is a need for achievable rate (inner bound) expressions rather than outer bounds. Inner bounds for this expression have not been developed at the time of the writing of this paper.

accepted.question_text: Under exactly what physical, angular, and surface-design conditions are RIS-induced channels reciprocal or non-reciprocal, and what validated theory or experimental evidence is needed to support communication-system models that assume a non-reciprocal RIS?

evidence.quote: A resolution of the differences between these results, and a conclusive determination of the conditions under which RIS-induced channels are reciprocal or non-reciprocal, will be welcomed. The system model and applications for a non-reciprocal RIS may be of interest in future applications, but is in need of verifiable theory and/or experimental evidence.

accepted.question_text: Can an RIS channel model be derived that keeps the end-to-end channel in a factored form GΦH, while still capturing mutual impedances and coupling by allowing the RIS matrix Φ to become a possibly non-diagonal function of circuit parameters, and can a practical channel-estimation method be built for that model?

evidence.quote: A more interesting and useful model is one that retains the factored form GΦH, separating the statistical part of the Tx-RIS and RIS-Rx channels, but incorporating the effects of mutual impedances and coupling into the RIS matrix Φ, making it potentially non-diagonal and function of circuit model parameters. Obtaining such a factored model and the associated estimation technique is a potential direction for future research.

accepted.question_text: Is perfect deactivation of RIS elements physically feasible for communication systems that need to suppress all RIS reflections during channel estimation, and if so, what electromagnetic design conditions and implementation methods make that feasible in a conclusive and communication-relevant way?

evidence.quote: the question of its physical feasibility remains unresolved.

To the best of the authors’ knowledge, no currently-available study in the open literature offers an in-depth and conclusive treatment of the feasibility of perfect deactivation of RIS elements and related design issues.

accepted.question_text: If RIS elements cannot be perfectly deactivated in practice, how does imperfect deactivation change the accuracy and robustness of channel-estimation methods that assume complete absorption, complete transmission, or complete removal of RIS reflections?

evidence.quote: Also, analyzing the effect of imperfect deactivation on the accuracy of estimation methods is an important future direction for research.

accepted.question_text: Can hardware structures that provide near-independent control of reflection amplitude and phase be shown to work effectively for RIS-aided communication systems, rather than only in related reflectarray or metasurface settings?

evidence.quote: A few studies in reflectarrays and meta surfaces [99], [102]–[104] aim at designing structures that allow near-independent control of reflection amplitude and phase, however, their applicability to RIS-aided communication has not been established.

accepted.question_text: Do the wideband remedies proposed in the reflectarray literature, such as true time-delay lines or multiple resonance elements, actually transfer to RIS-aided communication systems, and under what operating assumptions would they preserve useful beamforming behavior across the communication band?

evidence.quote: Several remedies have been proposed in the neighboring literature in reflectarrays, e.g., coupling the elements to true time delay lines [106] or by coupling multiple resonance elements [107]–[109]. The applicability of these methods for RIS-aided communications is yet to be explored, and is a direction for future study.

accepted.question_text: What channel models and channel-estimation techniques are appropriate for RIS-aided near-field communication, where a large RIS violates the far-field planar-wave assumption and different RIS elements experience different angles and polarization conditions?

evidence.quote: Without the far-field assumption, the incident waves at different elements will have unequal angular directions and polarization.
Studying suitable channel models and associated estimation techniques for RIS-aided near field communication is a potential direction for future research.
